newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds pare some losses as currency steadies.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds pare some losses as currency steadies.

text.p: Irish bonds recouped some of their earlier losses towards the close of business on Wednesday taking some comfort from a more stable currency after a sell-off of the punt earlier, dealers said.
"Bonds have recovered a bit of ground after the statement by Ruairi Quinn which appears to have given the punt a bit of stability," one bond dealer said.

He said finance minister Quinn's comments that the punt did not 'necessarily' have to join EMU at the central rate, which at current levels would imply a drop to 2.41 marks, put a bit 'of a bid' back into the market.
By 1715 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was down 10 pence to 101.85 to yield 5.95 percent, having fallen 50 pence from Tuesday's close to 101.45 to yield 6.11 by midday Wednesday.
The eight percent bond due 2006 closed up 10 pence by the close at 108.60 to yield 6.65 percent having fallen 43 pence from the close to 108.10 to yield 6.79 percent during the first session.
"We have got a better tone back into the market since Quinn's statement. Before that we had nothing to go on and the market does not like that kind of uncertainty," the dealer said.
He said the key thing now was what kind of tolerance the central bank had to a lower currency.
"If the punt falls against sterling and the mark and goes lower on a trade-weighted basis what will the central bank reaction to that be," he said.

"Effectively the central bank is making a bet on sterling that the British currency is going to fall. If they are wrong the consequences of that could be a significantly lower currency for Ireland and higher rates."

The Irish pound succumbed to strong selling pressures which had been building in anticipation of Ireland's perceived desire to enter European Monetary Union (EMU) at the median rate of 2.41 marks early on Wednesday.

Economists said rumours that Ireland's central bank, which had been intervening heavily to shore up the Irish unit in recent weeks, had decided to let the currency fall filtered through the market late on Tuesday.
The rumour opened the floodgates for large volume, mainly foreign, selling of the punt, traders said earlier.
Trading calmed in both currency and bond markets after Quinn told RTE that Ireland will not necessarily mean to join EMU at the central rate which is already there.
"No decision has been taken yet with regards to the rate at which we will join (EMU)," Quinn told Ireland's national broadcaster.
